strengths: The paper addresses a well-recognized and important problem in discrete diffusion language models (the conditional token independence bias that causes incoherent parallel sampling), and the proposed CoDiLA design—delegating local coherence to a compact soft-conditioned auxiliary AR model—is a clean, sensible hybrid that retains bidirectional/infilling capabilities that competing left-to-right coherence methods sacrifice.

The theoretical analysis is coherent and honestly scoped: the authors acknowledge that variants of the NELBO gap result exist in prior work and clearly state their incremental contribution (block size B > 1 and an explicit quantification of B_1 - B_B via total correlation within blocks). Theorem 3.3 motivates soft-conditioning over top-k truncation and is validated empirically by the soft vs. top-1 ablation (Table 1), which shows large accuracy drops for hard conditioning.

Experiments support the central claims: Figure 4 shows a consistent Pareto improvement in Pass@1 vs. throughput over both the Dream-Coder baseline and the direct competitor ADJUST across six benchmarks, and Figure 5 shows dynamic parallelism can retain base-model accuracy at >2x speedup.

Reproducibility is above average: the appendix provides complete training/evaluation details (dataset, hyperparameters, hardware, tokenizer/sentinel-ID alignment quirks, extraction protocol modifications, entropy-based unmasking algorithm), and all components use publicly available models and weights.

The paper is candid about design limitations, e.g., the candidate-scoping heuristic motivated by premature EOS prediction, and includes an ablation (Table 2) showing its effect on throughput, correctly concluding the speedup comes from the parallel block formulation rather than the reduced search space.
weaknesses: The experimental comparison is narrow. The only external baseline is ADJUST (Bansal & Sanghavi, 2025); several related and relevant efficiency methods discussed in the related work (Fast-dLLM/Fast-dLLM2, TiDAR, APD, semi-AR block diffusion, discrete copula diffusion) are not empirically compared. The authors argue these approaches differ in capability (e.g., infilling), but the Pareto-frontier claim would be considerably stronger with at least one such baseline on the accuracy-throughput plot.

Scope is limited to a single DLM (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B), a single domain (code), and batch size 1 on a single GPU. Whether the method transfers to other DLMs or general text generation is not demonstrated, and the reported speedups (2x dynamic, modest TPS in static mode) are not dramatic given the added 0.6B AR model and per-block AR decoding overhead.

The abstract's claim that a compact AR model 'effectively eliminates coherence artifacts' overstates the results: static results show substantial accuracy degradation at higher parallelism (e.g., HumanEval drops from ~74% to 29.9% at B=8), and accuracy only recovers when dynamic parallelism degrades toward sequential decoding.

The theoretical contributions are incremental: Theorem 3.2 is a direct block-granularity extension of existing total-correlation results the authors themselves cite (Huang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2025a; Kang et al., 2026; Zhong et al., 2026), and Theorem 3.3's sufficiency argument relies on an existence claim via universal approximation/Sklar's theorem that is somewhat idealized (as the authors concede in Remark 3.4, a single shared phi cannot implement per-instance copulas).

Empirical rigor has gaps: results are single-sample (n=1) with a fixed seed and no variance/confidence estimates across benchmarks; the NELBO theory is validated only via training loss on code SFT data (Figure 3) rather than held-out likelihood; and a separate AR model must be finetuned for each block size, which adds practical cost that is not discussed in the limitations.

strengths: The problem is well motivated and clearly framed: parallel sampling in masked DLMs samples independent marginals, causing local incoherence, and the paper positions CoDiLA as a hybrid that delegates local dependency modeling to a compact (0.6B) auxiliary AR model while preserving global, non-left-to-right diffusion benefits.

The soft-conditioning interface (projecting DLM marginals into the AR model's embedding space, Eq. 4) is a sensible and reusable design, and the soft vs. top-1 conditioning ablation (Table 1) directly supports the claim that the full marginal is a useful signal, consistent with Theorem 3.3's intuition.

The paper is unusually candid about the novelty boundary of its theory: it acknowledges that variants of the block-NELBO result existed (Huang et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2025a; Kang et al. 2026; Zhong et al. 2026) and claims only the B > 1 generalization and quantification of the gap, which the appendix proof handles cleanly via total correlation.

The empirical study includes useful engineering detail (candidate scoping ablation in Table 2, hyperparameters, hardware, decoding procedure in Appendix A), and the dynamic parallelism result (>2x speedup while roughly retaining base accuracy, Figure 5) is a practical contribution.
The limitations of the mechanism are discussed honestly in places (e.g., EOS instability motivating candidate scoping, accuracy degradation at larger static block sizes).
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are supported by a narrow evaluation: a single base model (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B), a single domain (code), and batch size 1 on one A100. The headline claim of a 'new Pareto frontier for accuracy and speed' is only established against the base DLM and ADJUST; strong and directly relevant inference frameworks that the paper itself cites (Fast-dLLM/v2, dInfer, D2F, TiDAR, copula diffusion) are not compared empirically, so the Pareto claim is not established against the actual state of the art.

The theoretical contributions are incremental. Theorem 3.2 is an acknowledged extension of known factorization-gap results, and Theorem 3.3's 'sufficiency' follows essentially from a universal-approximation/Sklar's-theorem existence argument — a statement about an existence of a per-instance parameterization that, as the authors concede in Remark 3.4, does not hold for a single shared learned phi. The link between the block-NELBO theory (which assumes the DLM itself outputs block-joint distributions) and the actual system (a frozen token-level DLM plus a separately trained AR model) is loose, so the theory provides weaker support for the method than the framing suggests.

The system in practice reintroduces much of the sequential structure it claims to avoid: greedy frontier-based unmasking with a 10-block candidate horizon effectively imposes a quasi-left-to-right order, and the paper's own ablation (Table 2) shows accuracy drops further when the horizon is widened. The distinction from the left-to-right methods criticized in Section 5 is thinner than claimed, and bidirectionality benefits are never directly demonstrated (e.g., no infilling experiments).

Static parallelism at the useful speeds shows substantial accuracy degradation (e.g., B=8: 29.9% vs. 68.9% Pass@1 on HumanEval in Table 1), and absolute throughputs are modest (18–80 TPS). The 'eliminates coherence artifacts' claim in the abstract overstates what the results show.

Evaluation rigor concerns: all results are single-sample, single-seed with no variance or significance reporting; Figure 3 validates the block-size theory only via training loss under a non-standard masking scheme, not via likelihood or downstream metrics; and the 'improved extraction logic' implemented for MBPP inside lm-evaluation-harness raises comparability questions — it is unclear whether baseline numbers use the same extraction protocol, which could inflate CoDiLA's relative standing.

Reproducibility is only partial: implementation details are commendably thorough, but no code release or checkpoint availability is stated, and the method requires per-block-size AR fine-tuning (32k steps each), which complicates independent verification.

Writing and claim calibration issues: the abstract and contributions assert strong, general results ('effectively eliminates coherence artifacts', 'new Pareto frontier') that the narrow evidence base does not fully carry, and there is no explicit limitations section.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-documented and important problem — the conditional independence bias in parallel sampling of masked diffusion LMs — with a clear and practical hybrid solution: a frozen DLM provides global marginals while a compact pretrained AR model (Qwen3-0.6B) performs locally coherent decoding within bounded blocks, preserving sub-linear latency and non-causal DLM capabilities.

The soft-conditioning interface (projecting DLM marginals into the AR model's embedding space) is a neat and lightweight mechanism, and the ablation in Table 1 (soft vs. hard top-1 conditioning) provides convincing evidence that the full distributional signal matters, empirically supporting Theorem 3.3.

The theoretical framing is honest: Theorem 3.2 (block-wise factorization reduces the achievable NELBO by the total correlation within blocks) and Theorem 3.3 (top-k truncation can exclude the global mode) are clearly stated, and the authors explicitly credit prior work (Huang et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2025a; Kang et al., 2026) for related statements rather than overclaiming novelty.

Experiments cover multiple standard code benchmarks (HumanEval/+, MBPP/+, BigCodeBench full/hard), compare against the closest competitor (ADJUST) using official weights, and show a consistent Pareto improvement in the accuracy-throughput trade-off. Dynamic parallelism (Figure 5) meaningfully mitigates the accuracy degradation of large blocks while retaining >2× speedup, which strengthens the practical case.

The appendix is unusually detailed regarding training protocol, tokenizer mismatch handling, evaluation pipelines (including the revised MBPP extraction logic), hyperparameters, and hardware, supporting reproducibility. The candidate-scope ablation (Table 2) is a commendable attempt to rule out the alternative explanation that speedup comes merely from a reduced search space.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is incremental: the paper itself acknowledges that variants of Theorem 3.2 exist in prior work, and the extension to blocks B > 1 follows from a direct entropy decomposition (the proof is a short total-correlation argument). Theorem 3.3's sufficiency proof relies on an informal universal-approximation/coupling existence argument ('there exists a parameterization φ'), which does not establish that such φ is learnable from data — a caveat the authors only note in Remark 3.4.

Evaluation is confined to a single base DLM (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) and a single domain (code generation). No results on general text generation, no second backbone (e.g., LLaDA or DiffuCoder), and no evidence the gains transfer beyond coding, which limits claims of generality for the method.

Baseline coverage is incomplete: Fast-dLLM, dInfer, and other block-based/semi-AR acceleration frameworks are discussed in Related Work but not compared empirically, even though they also target the accuracy-throughput Pareto front. The claim of a 'new Pareto frontier' is only established against the vanilla DLM and ADJUST. All throughput measurements are batch-size 1; batched throughput — where AR overhead amortizes differently — is not reported.

There is a visible tension the paper does not fully resolve: larger blocks reduce training loss (Figure 3) and are motivated by the theory, but static inference accuracy degrades substantially at B=8 (e.g., 29.9 vs. 68.9 Pass@1 on HumanEval at B=2). The dynamic scheme helps, but the mechanism by which aggressive parallelism hurts accuracy (error compounding across blocks?) is not analyzed or ablated.

Some methodological choices appear heuristic and are only partially justified: the candidate horizon of 10 blocks is admitted to trade accuracy for stability (premature EOS), the fallback to DLM confidence for k=1, and the block-mask training schedule with t ∼ Uniform(0.2, 0.8). These design decisions accumulate and are individually under-ablated.

No explicit statement of code release or artifact availability; given the many implementation-specific details (vLLM configuration, extraction logic, tokenizer-ID quirks), reproducibility would depend heavily on released code.

Minor overstatement: 'strictly improves the achievable NELBO' holds only when within-block total correlation is non-zero; the proof establishes B1 − BB ≥ 0, with strictness conditional on dependence within blocks.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-documented, practically important problem: the conditional token independence bias in masked diffusion LMs that causes incoherent parallel decoding. The proposed solution (a compact auxiliary AR model soft-conditioned on the DLM's marginals, restricted to short blocks) is a clean and sensible design that preserves the sub-linear latency goal and the DLM's bidirectional capabilities.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough for the main claims: six code-generation benchmarks, three generation modes (static, dynamic, verifier), comparisons against the base model and a direct competitor (ADJUST), and targeted evidence that gains come from coherence (Table 1 syntax error reduction) rather than the AR model's standalone ability (Qwen3-0.6B comparison).

Ablations are unusually complete: soft vs. Top-K conditioning, boundary tokens, AR model size (0.6B/1.7B/4B), candidate scope, multi-block generation, any-order generation analysis (Spearman correlation), and batch-size throughput. These support the design choices and the claim that performance does not rely on a strong AR backbone.

Reproducibility is good: code is stated to be released, and Appendix A gives detailed training/evaluation setups (data, hyperparameters, tokenizer-ID alignment details, hardware, extraction-protocol fixes).

Experiments on non-causal tasks (HumanEval-Infilling, ParallelBench, graph traversal) demonstrate the method does not reduce the DLM to a quasi-AR model, which is the key differentiator from left-to-right coherence-enforcement baselines.

The theory, while not deep, is honestly scoped: the authors explicitly acknowledge Theorem 3.2 is an extension of known results to blocks > 1, and the Top-K exclusion counterexample (Appendix D) is concrete and correct.
weaknesses: Theorem 3.3's sufficiency claim (point 1) is technically problematic. The proof invokes Sklar's theorem, but uniqueness of the copula decomposition holds only for continuous marginals; for discrete distributions the copula is non-unique. More fundamentally, two different joint distributions can share the same marginals, so q is not a function of π, and a single parameterization conditioned on π cannot recover arbitrary q. Remark 3.4 tacitly concedes this, which undercuts the 'necessary and sufficient' framing.

The soft-conditioning interface itself contradicts the spirit of the sufficiency argument: the expected embedding e_t = Σ π_v E(v) is a first-moment projection that is many-to-one in π, so the 'full marginal information' that Theorem 3.3 argues is necessary is not actually transmitted to the AR model. The paper never discusses this lossy compression of higher-order distributional information.

Evidence for the central Pareto-frontier claim is limited in scope: all main results use a single base model (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) and a single domain (code). Other strong efficiency baselines (Fast-dLLM/dInfer-style caching, block-diffusion approaches) are discussed in Related Work but not compared empirically, so 'new Pareto frontier' is established only within a narrow baseline set.

Absolute speed/accuracy trade-offs are modest: in the static regime, even CoDiLA B=2 loses ~5.5 pp on HumanEval for a roughly 2–3× throughput gain, and at higher parallelism accuracy degrades sharply (e.g., 29.9% vs. 74.4% sequential at ~6× TPS). The clean result (accuracy preserved at 2× with dynamic parallelism) relies on threshold tuning (τ) that is not systematically ablated.

HumanEval/MBPP are small (164/427 problems) and evaluation is single-sample with a fixed seed and no variance estimates or confidence intervals, making small Pass@1 differences (which drive several claims, e.g., Top-5 vs. Softmax in Table 4) hard to interpret statistically.

The modified masking protocol used in the block-size loss study (Figure 3) deviates from standard stochastic masking, and the 'no diminishing returns up to B=32' observation is then set aside because inference uses B ≤ 8; the connection between training-loss gains and downstream accuracy across block sizes is not directly established.

There is no explicit limitations section; limitations (fixed block sizes, extra 0.6B model and its batch-1 latency penalty, reliance on a shared tokenizer between DLM and AR, single-domain evidence) must be inferred from the text.

Some presentation issues: the headline abstraction (Figure 1) uses a simplified/cherry-picked illustrative example (acknowledged in the caption), and several key quantitative claims (e.g., '>2× speedup preserving accuracy' in dynamic mode) depend on reading values off small figures rather than reported tables.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and timely problem: the conditional independence bias of parallel sampling in masked diffusion language models, and the proposed hybrid DLM+local-AR design (CoDiLA) is a sensible and clearly articulated solution that preserves bidirectional/infilling capabilities better than left-to-right coherence-enforcement alternatives.

The theoretical framing is coherent: Theorem 3.2 formalizes the NELBO gap between block-wise and token-wise factorization via total correlation, and Theorem 3.3 motivates the soft-conditioning interface over top-k truncation. The proofs in Appendix D are correct at the level presented, and the authors are appropriately transparent that variants of Theorem 3.2 exist in prior work.

The empirical evaluation is broad for the code domain: HumanEval/MBPP (+ plus versions), BigCodeBench (full/hard), HumanEval-Infilling, ParallelBench, and a graph-traversal planning task, with syntax-error analysis (Table 1) that directly supports the coherence-improvement claim.

Ablations are extensive and honestly reported: soft vs. top-K conditioning, boundary-token removal, AR model size (0.6B/1.7B/4B), candidate scope, single vs. multiple blocks, any-order Spearman analysis, and batch-size throughput. The AR size ablation is a particularly good check against the objection that gains come from a strong AR backbone.
Appendix A provides unusually detailed reproducibility information (optimizer settings, tokenizer sentinel-ID mismatches, masking schedule, extraction-logic fixes), which is commendable.
weaknesses: Limited statistical rigor. All headline Pass@1 numbers are single-sample (n=1), fixed-seed evaluations on 164-problem HumanEval and similar-scale MBPP. Differences of a few points (e.g., CoDiLA 68.9 vs. ADJUST or baseline at matched throughput) are reported without confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests. This is a recurring issue in the field, but the paper's central claims of Pareto improvements hinge on small margins.

The theoretical contributions are largely derivative and their practical relevance is thin. The authors themselves concede that variants of Theorem 3.2 were already given by Huang et al. (2022), Liu et al. (2025a), Kang et al. (2026), and Zhong et al. (2026); the extension to B>1 is an incremental generalization. Theorem 3.3's sufficiency claim rests on the universal-approximation assumption of the AR model (Sklar's theorem + universal approximator), which is a weak guarantee that does not establish that the trained Qwen3-0.6B actually implements the required copula.

Only one base DLM (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) is studied. All main claims about establishing a Pareto frontier rest on a single backbone; no evidence is given that the approach transfers to other DLMs (e.g., LLaDA variants, DiffuCoder), which limits the significance of the contribution.

Potential confound from training data: the AR model is finetuned on Ling-Coder-SFT, the same SFT dataset used for Dream-Coder. The standalone finetuned Qwen3-0.6B achieves 35% on HumanEval, so part of the measured gains could reflect dataset-specific knowledge injected into the AR component rather than improved coherence per se. The Qwen-alone comparison partially addresses this, but a control with an AR model trained on disjoint data is missing.

The accuracy–latency gains are modest in absolute terms. Under dynamic parallelism the speedup is ~2x at preserved accuracy (Figure 5); under static parallelism accuracy still degrades substantially relative to sequential decoding (e.g., 68.9 vs. 74.4 on HumanEval at B=2). Compared to strong parallel-inference frameworks (Fast-dLLM, block diffusion approaches) that the paper acknowledges are compatible but does not benchmark against, the practical benefit is unproven.

Training/inference mismatch is under-analyzed: the AR model is trained with block-masking using DLM marginals from a synthetic masking schedule, but at inference the conditioning marginals come from the DLM's actual reverse process and different confidence states. No analysis of this distribution shift is provided.

Engineering complexity and overhead: a separate AR model must be finetuned for each block size, the method adds a second full model at inference (batch-size-1 throughput penalty, Table 8), and the pipeline depends on tokenizer-ID alignment hacks between Dream and Qwen vocabularies. These practical costs weaken the scalability story relative to training-free acceleration methods.

The claimed Pareto dominance over the base DLM is not uniformly convincing: in Figures 4 and 7, several CoDiLA operating points lie close to or below the baseline curve at low-throughput settings, and the Appendix B.4 result that one B=8 block beats two B=4 blocks suggests the method's benefit is largely confined to moderate parallelism.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-recognized and important problem in discrete diffusion language models: parallel sampling under conditional token independence produces locally incoherent text. The framing ('good at global drafting, bad at local coherence') is clear and motivating.

The proposed method (CoDiLA) is well-motivated and clean: a small frozen-DLM-compatible auxiliary AR model, soft-conditioned on the DLM's marginal distributions via expected embeddings, restricted to short blocks. This preserves the DLM's bidirectional/non-causal capabilities while fixing local coherence, which is a genuine design distinction from ADJUST, APD, and block-diffusion approaches that force quasi-AR behavior.

The empirical evaluation is thorough: static and dynamic parallelism regimes across HumanEval/MBPP/BigCodeBench (+ variants), infilling (HumanEval-Infilling), ParallelBench, and graph traversal, with consistent Pareto improvements over both the base DLM and ADJUST. The syntax-error reduction analysis (Table 1) directly supports the coherence mechanism claim.

The ablation suite is unusually complete and honest: soft vs. top-K conditioning, AR model size (0.6B/1.7B/4B showing no benefit from larger AR), candidate scope, multiple-block decoding, any-order analysis via Spearman correlation, and batch-size amortization of the AR overhead. The comparison against a standalone Qwen3-0.6B convincingly rules out the trivial explanation that the AR model alone accounts for the gains.

Theoretical results are relevant: Theorem 3.2 quantifies the NELBO reduction from block-level factorization via total correlation, and Theorem 3.3 gives sufficiency of full-marginal conditioning plus a concrete counterexample showing top-k truncation excludes the global mode. The counterexample proof (Roger/Roger) is crisp. Empirical loss curves (Figure 3) match the theory.

Reproducibility appears strong: code availability is stated, and Appendix A gives detailed training/decoding specifics (datasets, hyperparameters, tokenizer alignment details, extraction-logic revisions, vLLM configuration).
weaknesses: There is a gap between the theory and the actual mechanism: Theorem 3.3's sufficiency result assumes the AR model is conditioned on the full marginal vectors π, but the practical interface compresses each marginal to a single expected embedding (Eq. 4). Expected embedding is itself a lossy projection (it is a first-moment statistic, not a sufficient statistic for π), so the same 'exclusion' critique raised against top-k truncation could partially apply to soft embeddings. The paper never justifies theoretically why the expectation preserves enough information for copula recovery; the defense is purely empirical (Table 4).

The theoretical novelty is limited: the paper itself concedes that variants of Theorem 3.2 were already given by Huang et al. (2022), Liu et al. (2025a), Kang et al. (2026), Zhong et al. (2026); the contribution is extending to block size B>1 and quantifying the gap, which is incremental.

The DLM backbone is frozen with token-wise marginals; the 'block diffusion' framing is realized only through contiguous-block masking and the AR readout. The connection between the NELBO theory (about block-factorized denoisers) and the actual two-stage marginal-then-AR pipeline is looser than the presentation suggests.

Generality is untested beyond one base model (Dream-Coder-Instruct-7B) and one domain (code). All headline results are Python code benchmarks; claims about DLMs in general (e.g., natural language generation) remain extrapolative. The planning results use a tiny 6M-parameter synthetic setup, which is a weak proxy.

Pass@1 is reported from single-sample, fixed-seed runs without variance estimates or multiple seeds; several comparisons (e.g., 62.5 vs. 62.5 for DreamOn with different token budgets, or small ParallelBench gaps) rest on differences that could be within noise.

The AR component adds a second finetuned model per block size and a serialization step inside each denoising iteration; at batch size 1 there is a real throughput penalty (Table 8), and the wall-clock benefit depends on the batch-size amortization argument, which the main Pareto figures somewhat downplay.

The EOS/termination handling (local scope restriction, EOS top-1 penalty, hard EOS replacement at boundaries) is a collection of heuristics whose interaction is not analyzed; the degradation with larger scope (Table 5) shows this part of the system is fragile.
